Neonates of the bandy-bandy, Vermicella annulata, emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs after a developmental period lasting ninety-eight days [ab = ninety-eight days] when incubated at a constant temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. At the moment of hatching, these young-of-year reptiles display a snout–vent length averaging 17 centimeters [Lb = 17 centimeters]. Their corresponding body mass at this same life stage is quite modest, typically registering at 1.29 grams [Wwb = 1.29 grams], a value that underscores the slender, vermiform morphology characteristic of the genus. This initial mass is consistent with the species’ fossorial habits and relatively small clutch sizes, as the allocation of yolk resources is partitioned among a limited number of offspring per reproductive event. The incubation duration itself, which is prolonged relative to some other elapids of equivalent body size, likely reflects the thermal sensitivity of embryonic development in this lineage.

As individuals progress through the juvenile and sub-adult phases, significant dimorphism in somatic growth becomes apparent between the sexes. For female bandy-banded snakes, the ultimate snout–vent length attained by sexually mature adults reaches 54.4 centimeters [Li = 54.4 centimeters]. Males, in contrast, achieve a considerably smaller asymptotic body length of 39.2 centimeters [Li = 39.2 centimeters], a difference that likely stems from divergent selective pressures on reproductive roles. This degree of sexual size dimorphism, with females outgrowing males by a substantial margin, is a common pattern among ophidian taxa where fecundity selection favors larger body cavities to accommodate greater litter volumes. The adult body mass corresponding to the larger female ultimate length has been estimated at approximately 42 grams [Wwi = approximately 42 grams], a figure derived from morphometric relationships linking length to girth in this elongate species.

The onset of reproductive capability, marking the transition from an immature organism to a reproductively viable adult, occurs at different body sizes depending on sex. Female Vermicella annulata attain puberty once they reach a snout–vent length of 35.5 centimeters [Lp = 35.5 centimeters], a size threshold that presumably reflects the minimum abdominal volume necessary for successful gestation of a litter. Males, by contrast, achieve sexual maturity at the smaller size of 29 centimeters [Lp = 29 centimeters]. This disparity in size at maturation mirrors the ultimate size dimorphism and suggests that males can become reproductively active earlier in their growth trajectory, potentially allowing them to compete for mating opportunities before they have completed somatic expansion. The physiological triggers for this maturation event are likely linked to both endogenous hormonal cycles and the attainment of sufficient nutritional reserves.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for individuals of this species is approximately twelve years [am = approximately twelve years]. This longevity figure, representing the duration from the moment of egg fertilisation to natural mortality, is relatively high for a snake of such modest adult dimensions and may be linked to the species’ low metabolic rate and secretive, fossorial lifestyle that minimizes exposure to predation. The attainment of such an extended lifespan under captive conditions, where food availability is consistent and predators are absent, provides a useful benchmark for understanding the species’ intrinsic physiological limits. It is worth noting that wild individuals likely experience considerably shorter lifespans due to environmental hazards, but the captive data offer a valuable reference for the maximum biological potential of the species.

Gravid females of Vermicella annulata typically deposit a single clutch of leathery-shelled eggs per reproductive season, with the frequency of these nesting events being one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year]. Each clutch contains a modest number of offspring, generally between one and three eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between one and three eggs per clutch], a fecundity that is low compared to many other Australian elapids. This combination of a single annual reproductive event and a small clutch size yields a low overall annual reproductive output, a life-history strategy that is consistent with the species’ slow maturation and relatively extended maximum longevity. Such a pattern, characterized by delayed reproduction and low fecundity, aligns with the broader syndrome of a K-selected species adapted to stable, low-mortality environments, though the bandy-bandy’s precise demographic parameters in the wild remain the subject of ongoing field investigation.
